title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
authors: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, Yoshua Bengio

pages.title: The big idea
pages.subtitle: Let the decoder look back at the whole source

blocks.html: The question this page answers: the previous year’s seq2seq model squeezed an entire source sentence into a single fixed-length vector and asked the decoder to reconstruct the translation from it alone. This paper makes one sharp diagnosis — that fixed-length vector is a bottleneck — and proposes the mechanism we now call attention to remove it.

The analogy. Imagine translating a long paragraph by first reading it once, closing the book, and then writing the translation purely from memory. You would do fine on a short note but badly on a dense legal clause. A real translator instead glances back at the relevant phrase while writing each word. The fixed-vector model is the ‘close the book’ translator; attention lets the model glance back.

The fix concretely. Instead of forcing one summary vector to carry everything, keep all of the encoder’s per-word representations. As the decoder produces each target word, it builds a fresh context vector — a weighted blend of the source representations — that focuses on whichever source words are most relevant at that moment.

“Each time the proposed model generates a word in a translation, it (soft-)searches for a set of positions in a source sentence where the most relevant information is concentrated. The model then predicts a target word based on the context vectors associated with these source positions and all the previous generated target words.”

The headline result. The new model (called RNNsearch) matched the existing state-of-the-art phrase-based system Moses on English-to-French, and — the telling part — the gains were concentrated exactly where the old model failed: on long sentences. A bonus was that the learned attention weights form an interpretable soft-alignment map you can plot and read.

Context & trivia. This score–normalize–blend pattern is the direct ancestor of the attention in the Transformer (“Attention Is All You Need”, 2017). It is arguably the single most consequential architectural idea in the path from RNN translation to modern large language models.

pages.title: The fixed-vector bottleneck
pages.subtitle: Why one summary vector isn't enough

blocks.html: The setup being criticized. In the original RNN encoder–decoder, the encoder reads the source $x = (x_1,\\dots,x_{T_x})$ and produces a single context vector $c$ — typically its last hidden state. The decoder then generates the whole translation conditioned only on $c$. Everything the decoder will ever know about the source must pass through that one vector.

Concrete example of the squeeze. Suppose $c$ has 1000 dimensions. For a 4-word sentence, that is 250 numbers per word — plenty. For a 50-word sentence it is 20 numbers per word, and the network must also encode word order and grammatical structure in the same 1000 slots. The early words of a long sentence get crushed to make room for the later ones.

The empirical symptom. The authors (and prior work by Cho et al.) observed that a basic encoder–decoder’s translation quality degrades rapidly as sentences grow longer. BLEU stays high up to roughly the typical training-sentence length, then falls off sharply — a clear fingerprint of a capacity bottleneck rather than a modeling error.

“A potential issue with this encoder–decoder approach is that a neural network needs to be able to compress all the necessary information of a source sentence into a fixed-length vector. This may make it difficult for the neural network to cope with long sentences.”

The conceptual move. Stop summarizing prematurely. Rather than committing to one impression of the whole sentence up front, let the model defer: keep a representation of every source position, and decide at each output step which positions matter. This is the difference between memorizing and looking back — and it is what the rest of the paper makes precise and differentiable.

pages.title: A bidirectional encoder of annotations
pages.subtitle: One vector per source word, not one per sentence

blocks.html: The goal of the encoder. Produce not one vector for the sentence but a sequence of vectors, roughly one rich vector per source word, all kept around for the decoder to consult. The authors call each one an annotation $h_j$.

Why bidirectional. A single forward RNN’s state at position $j$ only knows the words up to $j$. But the meaning of a word often depends on what comes after it (“bank” in “river bank” vs “bank account”). So the encoder is a bidirectional RNN: a forward RNN reads left-to-right giving states $\\overrightarrow{h}_j$, a backward RNN reads right-to-left giving $\\overleftarrow{h}_j$, and the two are concatenated:

Reading it term by term: $\\overrightarrow{h}_j$ summarizes the sentence up to and including word $j$ from the left; $\\overleftarrow{h}_j$ summarizes it from the right; stacking them gives $h_j$, a vector that sees the whole sentence but is most strongly influenced by the words around position $j$, because a recurrent state reflects nearby inputs most.

Concrete example. For the source “the European Economic Area”, the encoder emits four annotations $h_1,\\dots,h_4$. The annotation $h_3$ (“Economic”) carries a localized picture of that word together with its left and right neighbors, rather than a blurry average of the whole phrase. The full set $(h_1,\\dots,h_{T_x})$ is what the decoder will attend over.

Why this matters. By replacing one sentence vector with $T_x$ annotations, the encoder no longer has to decide in advance what to keep. The burden of selecting relevant information is shifted to the decoder, which can make that decision freshly for each output word — the heart of the next page.

pages.title: The attention mechanism, step by step
pages.subtitle: Score, normalize, blend

blocks.html: This is the heart of the paper. When the decoder is about to emit target word $i$, it performs three operations — score, normalize, blend — to build a custom view of the source for that one word.
Step 1 — score. Measure how well each source annotation $h_j$ matches the decoder’s current need, given its previous hidden state $s_{i-1}$:

Here $e_{ij}$ is the alignment score — how relevant source word $j$ is to producing target word $i$. The scorer $a$ is a small one-hidden-layer feed-forward network, $a(s_{i-1}, h_j) = v_a^{\\top}\\tanh(W_a s_{i-1} + U_a h_j)$, trained jointly with everything else. There is no separate alignment step and crucially no alignment labels.
Step 2 — normalize. Turn the raw scores into weights that sum to one, via a softmax over all source positions:

Here $\\alpha_{ij}$ is the attention weight: the fraction of attention target word $i$ pays to source word $j$, with $\\sum_j \\alpha_{ij} = 1$. A weight near 1 means ‘this source word is what I care about right now’; the denominator just rescales the exponentiated scores so they form a probability distribution.
Step 3 — blend. Form the context vector as the weighted sum of the annotations:

Here $c_i$ is a custom summary built fresh for target word $i$, made mostly of the annotations it attends to. The key contrast with seq2seq: $c_i$ changes at every output step. The decoder gets a different, targeted view of the source for every word it writes, instead of one frozen vector for the whole sentence.

pages.title: A worked example of attention
pages.subtitle: Watching the context vector form on a real sentence pair

blocks.html: Let us run the mechanism on a real pair. Source (English): the European Economic Area. Target (French): la zone économique européenne. Notice the reordering: English puts the adjectives before the noun (“European Economic Area”) while French puts “zone” first and the adjectives after (“zone économique européenne”). A rigid left-to-right model cannot express this swap; attention can.

Producing the second French word, ‘zone’ ($i=2$). The decoder scores each of the four annotations. The scorer fires most strongly on $h_4$ = “Area”, because “zone” translates “Area”. After softmax the weights might be roughly:

The context vector is then $c_2 = 0.04\\,h_1 + 0.06\\,h_2 + 0.10\\,h_3 + 0.80\\,h_4$ — overwhelmingly the “Area” annotation, with a little context from its neighbors. When the decoder later produces “économique” it will instead place most of its weight on $h_3$ = “Economic”, and for “européenne” on $h_2$ = “European”. The attention jumps backward through the source to follow the French word order — the model has learned the reordering with no alignment supervision.

Why ‘soft’ alignment. The model never commits hard to a single source word; it spreads a probability distribution $\\alpha_{ij}$ over all of them. That softness is exactly what makes the whole thing differentiable: gradients can flow back through the weighted sum and adjust the scorer, so the network learns where to look purely from the pressure to translate well.

pages.title: Decoding with a moving context
pages.subtitle: Each output word gets its own view of the source

blocks.html: How the context plugs into generation. The decoder is still a recurrent network, but its state and its output now depend on the step-specific context $c_i$ instead of one global vector. The probability of each target word is:

Reading it term by term: the probability of the $i$-th target word, given all previous target words and the whole source $x$, is computed by a function $g$ (a softmax output layer) from three inputs — the previously emitted word $y_{i-1}$, the decoder’s current hidden state $s_i$, and the freshly computed context $c_i$ that points at the relevant source words.
The state update uses the context too:

Here $s_i$ is the new decoder state, $f$ is the recurrent cell (the paper uses a gated unit / GRU), and the inputs are the previous state $s_{i-1}$, the previous output $y_{i-1}$, and the context $c_i$. Because a different $c_i$ is fed in at every step, the same recurrent machinery produces a sentence-position-aware translation.

Why it all trains end-to-end. Every operation — the scorer $a$, the softmax, the weighted sum, and the recurrent decoder — is differentiable. So the entire model, encoder and attention and decoder together, is trained by ordinary backpropagation to maximize the log-probability of the correct translation. Alignment is not annotated or pre-computed; it emerges as a byproduct of learning to translate.

pages.title: Setup and the headline numbers
pages.subtitle: RNNsearch vs RNNencdec vs Moses on WMT'14 En-Fr

blocks.html: The experimental setup. Both models were trained on the WMT’14 English-French corpus (about 348 million words after selecting a 348M-word subset), with a vocabulary of the 30,000 most frequent words in each language and all other words mapped to a special [UNK] token. The encoder and decoder each used 1000 hidden units; training used minibatch SGD with Adadelta and beam search at decoding time.

The two contenders. RNNencdec is the baseline fixed-vector encoder–decoder; RNNsearch is the new attention model. Each was trained twice: once on sentences up to 30 words (suffix ‘-30’) and once up to 50 words (‘-50’). RNNsearch-50* was trained much longer, until development-set performance stopped improving.

Reading the table. ‘All’ scores every test sentence; ‘no UNK’ restricts to sentences with no unknown word in source or reference. At every comparable setting, attention wins decisively — RNNsearch-50 beats RNNencdec-50 by nearly 9 BLEU on all sentences. And on the ‘no UNK’ subset, RNNsearch-50* reaches 36.15, actually edging past the mature Moses system at 35.63. A pure neural model matching phrase-based SMT was a landmark in 2015.

pages.title: Big gains on long sentences
pages.subtitle: Exactly where the bottleneck used to bite

blocks.html: The most telling plot. The paper plots BLEU against source-sentence length. The baseline RNNencdec’s quality falls off a cliff once sentences exceed roughly the length it was trained on (about 20–30 words). The attention model RNNsearch stays roughly flat well past fifty words.

“RNNsearch-50, especially, shows no performance deterioration even with sentences of length 50 or more. This superiority … is further confirmed by the fact that the RNNsearch-30 even outperforms RNNencdec-50.”

Why this is the smoking gun. Remarkably, RNNsearch-30 (trained only on short sentences) beats RNNencdec-50 (trained on long ones) even on long test sentences. The advantage is not about training data length — it is structural. Letting the decoder look back removes the need to compress a long sentence into one vector, which is precisely the failure the problem page diagnosed. This is direct confirmation that the fixed-vector bottleneck was the culprit.

pages.title: Attention as interpretable alignment
pages.subtitle: The weights line up with human intuition

blocks.html: A free bonus: interpretability. Because the attention weights $\\alpha_{ij}$ form a matrix indexed by source position $j$ and target position $i$, you can simply plot it as a grayscale image (white = high weight). The result is a soft alignment map showing which source words each output word drew from.

What the maps show. Mostly a bright near-diagonal — word $i$ in the target aligns with roughly word $i$ in the source — but with sensible, non-monotonic reorderings exactly where the two languages differ. In one of the paper’s examples, the English phrase “European Economic Area” aligns to the French “zone économique européenne” with the attention visibly crossing over to reverse the adjective order — the reordering worked through on the previous worked-example page, now confirmed by the model’s own weights.

“The strength of the soft-alignment, opposed to a hard-alignment, is evident … This kind of soft-alignment lets the model deal with the difference of word counts and orderings between the source and target languages.”

Why this mattered for adoption. Earlier neural translators were black boxes. Here you can see what the model is doing, debug it, and verify it learned linguistically sensible alignments — with no alignment labels ever provided. This visualizability is a large part of why attention spread so fast across NLP.

The lasting contribution. The score–softmax–blend pattern introduced here is the conceptual core of all modern attention. The paper found the one piece of the encoder–decoder that was doing the heavy lifting, gave it a clean differentiable form, and showed it could be learned end-to-end without supervision.

The line of descent. Three years later, “Attention Is All You Need” threw away the recurrent backbone entirely and kept only this mechanism, generalized into self-attention (where a sequence attends to itself) and stacked into the Transformer. The exact ‘query scores keys, softmax, weighted sum of values’ recipe in Transformers is this paper’s $e_{ij}$, $\\alpha_{ij}$, $c_i$ under new names.

The big picture. Read with hindsight, this is the hinge between the RNN era and the Transformer era. Everything from BERT to GPT inherits the idea that a model should learn, for each output, what to pay attention to. In this collection it sits directly downstream of seq2seq (whose bottleneck it removes) and directly upstream of the Transformer (which is built almost entirely from its attention).
